Effective sample size of a set of weights

Source: R/two_period_covs.R
effective_sample_size.Rd

Computes Kish's effective sample size, \((\sum_i a_i)^2 / \sum_i a_i^2\), for the weights of one group (call it separately for the treated and untreated groups), where \(a_i\) is unit \(i\)'s estimation weight times its sampling weight. It equals the number of units when all weights are equal and falls as the weights become more concentrated.

Usage

effective_sample_size(
  est_weights,
  sampling_weights = rep(1, length(est_weights))
)

Arguments

est_weights

A numeric vector of weights from an estimation procedure (e.g., implicit regression or AIPW weights) for one group. If these already include the sampling weights (as the AIPW weights in two_period_aipw_weights() do), leave sampling_weights at its default.

sampling_weights

A numeric vector of sampling weights for the same units. Default rep(1, length(est_weights)).

Value

A number: the effective sample size.

Details

The weight that enters the formula is the total weight each unit gets in the weighted mean, \(a_i = w_i s_i\), so the result is the usual Kish effective sample size of the weighted estimator: with homoskedastic outcomes, the weighted mean has the same variance as an unweighted mean of this many units. With sampling weights, it therefore reflects both the estimation weights and the sampling weights; when the estimation weights are all equal, it is the effective sample size of the sampling weights alone. The result does not depend on the scale of either set of weights.

Equivalently, with \(a_i\) normalized to have mean one across the \(n\) units, it is \(n / (\widehat{Var}(a) + 1)\), where the variance uses divisor \(n\); this is the per-cell formula in Caetano and Callaway (2026).

References

Kish, Leslie. Survey Sampling. Wiley (1965).

Caetano, Carolina and Brantly Callaway. "Difference-in-Differences when Parallel Trends Holds Conditional on Covariates." Working paper (2026). doi:10.48550/arXiv.2406.15288 .

Examples

effective_sample_size(rep(1, 50)) # 50: equal weights
#> [1] 50
effective_sample_size(c(rep(1, 45), rep(10, 5))) # concentrated weights
#> [1] 16.55963
# with sampling weights, the total weight of each unit is what matters
effective_sample_size(rep(1, 50), sampling_weights = c(rep(1, 45), rep(10, 5)))
#> [1] 50
